newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila T-bills market uneasy despite rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Manila T-bills market uneasy despite rate cut.

text.p: Trading in the Philippine secondary Treasury bill market remained cautious on Monday despite the three-percentage point cut in the central bank's short-term benchmark rates, traders said.
"Banks are still very cautious. Nobody wants to buy T-bills at this point. Everything is very fluid," one trader at a large commercial bank said.
He said uncertainties in the foreign exchange market still outweighed the three-percentage point reduction in benchmark rates announced mid-morning.
Speculation on regional currencies still persist making the peso vulnerable to fresh attacks.
The central bank offered a one-day reverse repo at 22 percent, effectively cutting its closely-watched overnight borrowing rate starting Tuesday to 22 percent from 25 percent.
It also trimmed its four-day, two-week and one-month reverse repo rates to 15 percent from 18 percent.
"We're still not sure whether the T-bill rates will come down, because banks can go either to the special short-term bills or lend their money to their clients," a trader from a foreign bank said.
The Bureau of Treasury is set to offer 35-day and 42-day bills on Tuesday. Yields on the special T-bills were higher than the regular three, six- and 12-month bills.
Offers for the three-month bills remain high between 13.10 to 13.5 percent, but there was no significant demand.
Commercial clients had shifted to special savings rate offered by some banks, which ranged from 16 to 17 percent for one-month deposits, he added.
The interbank call loan rate was unchanged at 25.03125 percent with turnover of 11.040 billion pesos.
